title: Finding a bug you cannot make happen
lead: Most bugs do not need this. If you can see it fail, write a test that fails the same way, fix it and move on. This guide is for the other kind: it happens to someone else, only sometimes, and never on your machine. The method is to make it fail on demand before you try to fix anything.
scenario: Pottery Studio Booking is an invented app. A few people say their class shows on the wrong day. The app, the three reports and the results are invented; the command output below came from a real run of a small sample script.
input: Some people see their pottery class on the wrong day. I cannot make it happen on any of our machines. Diagnose this.

steps.label: Check that this is the hard kind
steps.text: Ask one question first: can you make it fail right now? A typo on a button, a crash with a stack trace and a failing test someone already wrote are all easy, and they need a test and a fix, not this loop. Here, three people out of about four hundred report a wrong day and nobody on the team can see it. That is the hard kind.

steps.label: Build a signal that fails on demand
steps.text: Before any theory, make a command that fails every time. The three reports share two things: the people are in Europe or Australia, and the studio is in Denver. The team all sit in Denver. So the loop takes a stored class time and a viewer's time zone and prints the label the page would show. For a 19:00 class on 3 March, run from Denver, it prints the right day. Run from London, it does not.

steps.label: Shrink it to the smallest failure
steps.text: Strip away everything the failure does not need: the login, the database, the page, the cache. What is left is one function with two inputs, a stored instant and a viewer zone. Then find the edge. In London a class that starts at 16:59 studio time shows the right day, and one at 17:00 shows the next day. A bug with a sharp edge is easier to explain than one that happens sometimes.

steps.label: Rank guesses you can disprove
steps.text: Write four guesses, each with what it predicts and a test that would kill it. One: the day comes from the viewer's clock while the time comes from the studio's. Two: daylight saving shifts the hour. Three: the stored time is already wrong. Four: a cached page is served to the wrong viewer. Order them by how likely and how cheap to test.

steps.label: Look at the list before anything runs
steps.text: You may know something the list does not. Here you add that the studio's own staff never see it and that the clocks changed in neither country that week. That strengthens guess one and weakens guess two before a single test runs. You can also add a guess; you cannot let the agent pick the fix by itself.

steps.label: Test the guesses, one change at a time
steps.text: Each guess gets one test that changes one thing. Guess two dies: the failure shows up on 3 March, weeks from any clock change. Guess three dies: the stored times for the three bookings match their classes. Guess four dies: the same wrong day appears with the cache bypassed. Guess one makes a prediction nobody else made, that a New York viewer sees the right day, and it holds.

steps.label: Fix it with a test that fails first
steps.text: The failing case becomes the regression test: a London viewer and a 19:00 Denver class must show Tuesday. Watch it fail for the right reason. Then change the function to take the day from the studio's zone, the same zone the time already uses, and watch it pass. Add the 16:59 case beside it. This is the whole of the tdd step here; a small, clear fix would need nothing more.

steps.label: The bug note
steps.text: Four lines a later reader can use: what failed, the command that shows it, the cause and the test that now guards it.

steps.label: When no signal can be built
steps.text: Suppose none of the three people could say where they were, and no stored value for their bookings could be read. Then no honest signal exists yet. Stop and ask for one thing: one raw booking record, one affected person's time zone setting, or permission to add temporary logging. Do not guess a fix and call it done. Remove any secrets before sharing a record.

settled: The day label and the time label use different time zones.
Daylight saving, the stored data and the cache are not the cause.
open: Why only three of four hundred people reported it. A guess: most did not notice.
Whether any other page builds a label the same way.

artifact.title: Bug note (invented example)
lines: Failed: a 19:00 Denver class on Tuesday 3 March showed as Wednesday 4 March to viewers in London and Sydney.
Signal: TZ=Europe/London node label.js 2026-03-04T02:00:00Z printed 'Wed 4 Mar, 19:00'. The same run with TZ=America/Denver printed 'Tue 3 Mar, 19:00'.
Cause: the day was formatted in the viewer's time zone and the time in the studio's.
Guard: two tests, a London viewer at 16:59 and at 17:00 studio time, both expecting Tuesday.

stop: You are done when the command that failed now passes, the regression test fails on the old code and passes on the new, and the rest of the tests still pass. Stop earlier if you cannot build a failing signal: ask for access or an artifact instead of fixing a guess. A theory you like is not a stopping point.
limits: The app and its reports are invented, and the fix is a small one. A real fault may have several causes, may need data you cannot get, or may change when you observe it. This method does not make hard bugs easy; it stops you from fixing a bug you have not seen. diagnosing-bugs is the published skill, unchanged. My tdd copy differs slightly, and the registry says how. Most bugs need only a failing test and a fix.
